item: The extraction lock has a live gauge: seconds held and thread-seconds waited are kept as cumulative totals, so an open hold, an open wait and a pass that never ends are all readable
summary: lock_stats recorded a hold only when it ENDED and the pass monitor resets the window every pass, so a crashed pass, a hang or an 85 s hold left nothing to read. lock_stats now also keeps two cumulative totals for the life of the process (seconds the lock was held, thread-seconds spent waiting for it) behind a private leaf lock that reset() does not touch, and live_reading() adds the part of a hold and of each wait still open at the instant of the reading, with holder_age_s and the number waiting. Both totals only grow, so the difference of two readings is exact for the interval between them. extract_article marks asking (first statement of the outer try, before the lock), holding (first statement inside the hold), released (first statement of the finally inside the hold; it returns the clock reading, which is the hold's end stamp, so the pass window and the gauge end a hold at the same instant) and, through record(), gave_up (unconditional and idempotent: it closes a wait that holding never closed). The clock is read under the gauge's lock so a held fraction can never exceed the elapsed time. CPython 3.13 checks for a pending interrupt at a call's return, at the start of a Python frame and at a backward jump, so each of the four step bodies has none of those in it (no call, no loop, no with) and computes every new total BEFORE it stores any: a mark is applied whole or not at all, and a step that fails (MemoryError while allocating a float) changes nothing. A stale wait is closed at the thread's next ask and a phantom holder at the next hold taken by another thread, each keeping the totals continuous. Nothing reads the gauge yet (the monitor block waits for the governor PR). Proof: 31 tests, among them an eight-thread run checked against an independent log (a tape of the gauge's own clock reads, one labelled entry per mark, tolerance 1e-6), AST pins that the marks sit where the exception table needs them, a bytecode pin (dis) that no step body has a CALL, backward jump, loop, with or comprehension (with a positive control for the finder) and one test per step that an arithmetic failure leaves the state exactly as it was; 43 mutants (the first 29 re-made against the rewritten steps, plus loops, with-blocks and calls in a step body, stores ahead of the arithmetic in each step, and a record() that gives up only after its window update), all killed. Two independent Opus reads. The first (first head) found five defects: a waiter leaked when an interrupt landed between asking and the lock, so waited_s went backwards; the phantom-holder edge stated too narrowly and since left set at depth 0; a 64 KB claim the first A/B contradicted; three surviving mutants and a positional tape; a cost apportioned rather than measured. The delta read of that fold found seven more: a step stored before it computed (a failed addition left half a mark applied); a pin that looked only for calls and missed a backward jump; gave_up's place in record() not pinned (a failing window update could leave a waiter); a cost sentence the cross-check below contradicted; the gauge's assumption of an exclusive lock unstated; the same thread's next hold deepening a phantom instead of healing it; two wrong docstring sentences. All twelve are folded. Signal probe against a stub body with an interrupt every 1 to 40 microseconds: 190,638 interrupts in the author's run and 144,022 in the reviewer's, 0 leaked waiters and 0 holds left set at depth 0 in both, phantom holders in 6.3 and 7.6 percent of interrupts (an interrupt at a mark's own entry; inflated by construction, a real KeyboardInterrupt is one event). Cost, measured alone on the machine, micro-benchmark (warm, uncontended, three runs per head): on the head the pass-level A/B below ran on (76ef05e7e) the two marks inside the hold took 1.21 to 1.22 microseconds and all four marks 2.3 to 2.6; on THIS head, whose step bodies compute before they store, the pair takes 1.34 to 1.36 microseconds (+0.13, about 11 percent) and all four marks 2.52, against a 4.3 to 4.8 ms extraction of an 8 KB page on one thread (28.6 to 30.4 ms for 64 KB); the first machine gave 1.1, 1.1, 1.7 and 2.1 to 3.0; shared vCPUs, noisy. In situ, in the loaded run, the gap between the window's got stamp and the gauge's start of a hold was 2 to 6 microseconds per hold: that is what the part of holding() before its own clock read costs there, so it is a floor for the cost of the whole of holding() in a loaded run, which is more than the warm micro figure (that part alone is 0.005 to 0.015 percent of a 40 ms hold). Pass-level A/B, run on 76ef05e7e (the first fold, rebased on main 4460855d0) and NOT repeated on this head: the later step-body change is 0.13 microseconds per hold by the micro-benchmark, far below what a pass resolves; main moved by 9 files since 4460855d0 (quarantine, backup merge, host mismatch: none on the collector path). Real collector (run_scrape_once + EthicalFetcher + store + write gate over the in-process session double, zero network, SQLCipher, 14 collectors, lock on, pins trafilatura 2.1.0 / lxml 6.1.1, 4 shared vCPUs with the run pinned to two), base = main 4460855d0 against 76ef05e7e, five alternating runs per cell, median [min..max]: 8 KB pages 420 [412..442] articles/min on base against 424 [397..437] with the gauge, mean hold 39.8 against 40.4 ms, lock held share 28.4 against 28.0 percent; 64 KB pages 121 [116..126] against 120 [113..129] articles/min, mean hold 319 against 312 ms, mean wait 841 [790..919] against 872 [787..985] ms, held share 64.2 against 64.3 percent. Paired by run number (the two cells of a run ran back to back), fold over base: articles/min median 0.988 [0.964..1.048] at 8 KB and 0.988 [0.938..1.032] at 64 KB. No difference beyond the spread of five runs; throughput drifts down across the 64 KB runs on BOTH trees (base 126 to 116), so the order alternates and the pairs are the fair reading. A pass-level run cannot resolve a microsecond against a 35 to 320 ms hold and is not claimed to. Not clean, said plainly: the first A/B (the pre-fold gauge, three runs, an older base) read the longest single hold and longest single wait higher with the gauge at both sizes (8 KB: hold 0.75 against 0.56 s, wait 0.95 against 0.77 s; 64 KB: hold 2.74 against 2.66 s, wait 11.4 against 10.6 s) and an earlier draft of this row called that absent at 64 KB, which was wrong. In the second A/B the longest hold reads lower with the gauge (8 KB 0.81 against 0.85 s, 64 KB 2.86 against 3.01 s) and the longest wait about equal (0.84 against 0.82 s, 12.1 against 11.9 s), paired medians 0.75 and 0.95 for the hold, 1.05 and 1.01 for the wait. Each is one event per run, so the direction is not reproduced and the first reading is INFERRED to be scheduler noise on shared vCPUs, not shown; a small effect on a single event is not excluded. Cross-check on the ten gauge runs of the second A/B: the gauge's growth over the measured passes is below the pass windows' hold totals by 1.7 to 4.4 ms over totals of 26 to 251 s and within 2.2 ms of their wait totals over 69 to 709 s (the windows' totals are rounded to 1 ms), with nobody waiting and no holder at the end of any run. The hold side runs low because the gauge starts a hold at the holding mark's own clock read, a few microseconds after the window's got stamp (2 to 6 microseconds per hold over 720 holds, INFERRED from the size, not separately measured); both are floors of the lock's real occupancy, which began at the acquire and ended at the release. Known edges, stated in the code: the gauge assumes an exclusive lock (it means nothing with the no-op lock of the harness's lock-off cells); an unmatched release is clamped; an interrupt at a mark's own entry can still skip that mark; a skipped asking registers nothing and a skipped holding leaves a waiter that record() and the next asking close; a skipped (or failed) released leaves a phantom holder that the next holding from another thread closes, while the same thread's next holding DEEPENS it (its age grows while the lock is free and that thread's later holds are booked inside it) and a thread that reuses a dead holder's get_ident() value is not another thread, so both last until restart. Best effort, never an extraction's result. Not measured: lock off, other core counts, a store with real article history, real network time; only 8 and 64 KB bodies.
